newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban agree tentatively to join U.N. truce talks.
newsitem.headline: Taleban agree tentatively to join U.N. truce talks.

text.p: Leaders of Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia agreed in principle on Sunday to join U.N.-proposed ceasefire talks with rival factions, Taleban sources said.
U.N. envoy Norbert Holl flew to Kandahar to brief provincial governor Mullah Mohammad Hassan and acting Deputy Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Jalil on his proposal.
Holl has already secured agreement in principle for the ceasefire talks from anti-Taleban faction leaders Ahmad Shah Masood and General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
He plans to travel soon to the central city of Bamiyan to meet a Shi'ite Moslem faction leader, Karim Khalili, who is allied with Masood and Dostum against the Taleban.

A Taleban spokesman in Kandahar, contacted by telephone, said Holl had outlined his plan for a technical committee, made up of three representatives from the Taleban and three from the opposition, to discuss the modalities of a ceasefire.
The Taleban proposed that the committee meet in mid-January in Islamabad or in Ashgabat, capital of Turkmenistan.
Masood is thought to be reluctant to accept Islamabad as the venue because of his long-held belief that Pakistan is the main sponsor of the Taleban, a charge Islamabad denies.
"In principle we agree to the U.N. efforts, but we doubt that Masood is sincere," said the Taleban spokesman.
In Kabul, acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said earlier the Taleban would join the talks on condition that no action was taken against its administration or Islamic law.

"We have conditions for negotiations and a ceasefire," he told reporters. "Nobody should do anything against the establishment of the Islamic government which is already in place or oppose the implementation of sharia (Islamic law).
"If these points are accepted, we are ready for any kind of negotiations."

Mutaqi rejected as "irrational" an opposition demand that the capital should be demilitarised. "It is irrational because Kabul is already run by a police force. If anyone insists on this matter, it means they want further looting of Kabul.
"For the first time in 17 years Kabul is peaceful and we will not accept any deal which insists on the demilitarisation of the city," he said.
A U.N. official said the Taleban had promised to reply to the United Nations proposal soon, after discussing it in their Supreme Shura (council) based in the southern city of Kandahar.
Forces of Masood and Dostum are battling the Taleban militia north of Kabul and in the northwestern province of Badghis.
The Taleban captured Kabul on September 27, ousting the former government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani and prompting Masood and Dostum to form an alliance against the Taleban.
The Taleban want to impose their strict version of Islamic law across Afghanistan, ravaged by war for the past 17 years.
